newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian town gets back to basics - smuggling.
newsitem.headline: Albanian town gets back to basics - smuggling.

text.p: As night falls, this Albanian port's only profitable industry -- smuggling drugs and illegal emigrants to nearby Italy -- springs into life.
The bleak Adriatic town was the scene of bloody clashes last week between riot police and anti-government protesters who had lost their savings in failed investment schemes.
Now the criminal economy, for long the life-line in this impoverished southern region and a source of cash for ill-fated pyramid schemes, is enjoying a new boom.
Every night about a dozen speedboats make the crossing from Vlore to Italy, just 40 miles across the Adriatic, supplying a constant flow of drugs and cheap labour to the European Union.
Locals said some 60 speedboats were operating, each feeding 15 people -- the boat owner, his skipper, guards and middlemen.
Competition among the smugglers is becoming fiercer. During riots last week, people seized some 135 additional speedboats impounded by police in past crackdowns on illegal smuggling.
They raided the port of Radhime, eight km (five miles) south of Vlore, after police were driven off under a hail of stones in clashes last Monday and Tuesday.
At Radhime's dilapidated pier, a rusty crane hoist a wreck of a speedboat on to a truck to haul it to a workshop in Vlore, where smugglers will try to fix it.
"Police sunk at least 25 speedboats in this port," says the truck driver. "They stripped off the parts they could use, sold them and then submerged the boats."
The line between friend and foe in this shady business is blurred.
Selim, a man in his 40s who is watching the scene, says he does not want to be interviewed for fear of his life.
"I can't talk I'm afraid. All I can tell you is that this situation is really bad," he said before disappearing into a nearby shed.

A taxi driver explains Selim was paid by police to guard the impounded speedboats but smugglers paid him handsome bribes to turn a blind eye when they took boats out of the compound at night and returned them before sunset.
Local smugglers say Albanians pay about $500 for the short crossing to Italy's Puglia region. Kurds or Asians have to pay some $800 each since they require more work by middlemen.
"Police participated in bringing the more expensive refugees to the port and got their cut," one smuggler said.

Driven by big six-cylinder engines providing up to 250 horsepower, the boats can carry as many as 15 people. The return trip to Italy takes four hours, with some boats making the run two or three times a night.
In Triporti, north of Vlore, a skipper proudly pointed at his grey-coloured speedboat and said his craft was worth at least $60,000.
None of the boats assembled in the bay has navigation lights -- all the skippers need is sharp eyes to evade the Italian coast guard.
Besnik, 35 and a smuggler, said transporting clandestini (illegal emigrants) is better than drugs because they just have to be unloaded on shore and then they disappear into the woods.
"Sometimes we take drugs across, but in general we prefer clandestini," he said.
Late in the evening few residents dare to walk the town's streets for fear of the crime and violence that has engulfed Vlore over the past week.
Two lightly-clad women make their way along the port.
"They are just a couple of prostitutes going across to Italy for a few hours to make some money," explains Agim, a local taxi driver. "They'll be back before sunrise."
